title: Kenford Co. v. County of Erie
lead: A planned stadium prompts its prospective donor to invest in surrounding land. When the county abandons construction, the ensuing damages litigation asks whether the county guaranteed the hoped-for appreciation.

actors.name: Erie County
actors.role: Public entity promising to construct a domed stadium.

actors.name: Kenford Company and Edward Cottrell
actors.role: Landowner company and its president and sole shareholder, who acquired surrounding parcels.

actors.name: Dome Stadium, Inc. (DSI) and Roy Hofheinz
actors.role: Proposed stadium operator and the Astrodome developer who formed it with Cottrell.

proceedings: Liability was established by summary judgment, followed by a lengthy damages trial and multiple appeals.
A land-appreciation retrial produced a $6.5 million award affirmed by the Appellate Division.
The Court of Appeals reversed the relevant portions of the 1988 final and 1985 underlying orders and struck that award with costs.
limits: This historical account follows the canonical brief, not a new audit or later-law certification. The 1989 disposition removed peripheral-land appreciation, not every damages award. Its operative ground was lack of contemplated liability; the earlier DSI profits decision separately involved both contemplation and certainty. Editorial UCC comparisons are not holdings governing this agreement.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A stadium proposal becomes a land-and-operation bargain
sections.cue: Why did Kenford acquire land beyond the donated site?
paragraphs: In May 1968, Erie County authorized a domed sports stadium and $50 million in financing. Kenford Company, whose president and sole shareholder was Edward Cottrell, acquired options on Lancaster land and offered to sell the County a stadium site. The County declined.

Kenford then enlisted Roy Hofheinz, who had helped develop the Houston Astrodome. Hofheinz and Cottrell formed Dome Stadium, Inc., or DSI. Kenford proposed donating the site in exchange for DSI’s opportunity to lease or manage the stadium. The County accepted that proposal in June 1969, and Cottrell exercised options on surrounding parcels during negotiations.

The August 8 contract required Kenford to donate 178 acres for the stadium and access roads and required the County to begin construction within twelve months. The parties would negotiate a forty-year DSI lease expected to yield at least $63.75 million in revenues, including stadium taxes, rent, and increased taxes on peripheral land owned, contracted for, or later acquired by Cottrell or Kenford.
If no satisfactory lease emerged within three months, an attached twenty-year management agreement was to be executed. The forty-year lease was never agreed.

sections.title: Costs defeat construction and generate a large damages suit
sections.cue: Which losses did the first trial award?
paragraphs: Construction bids reached about $72 million, exceeding authorized financing by $22 million. Attempts to increase the appropriation failed. In January 1971, the County terminated the contract; Kenford’s alternative-financing efforts also failed.

Kenford and DSI sued in June for specific performance or $90 million, later increasing their damages demand to $495 million. Liability was established on summary judgment. A damages trial lasting roughly nine months awarded Kenford $18 million in anticipated surrounding-land appreciation and over $6 million in out-of-pocket expenses, and awarded DSI $25.6 million in expected twenty-year management profits.

sections.title: The first appeals narrow the dispute to raw-land appreciation
sections.cue: What was before the Court of Appeals in 1989?
paragraphs: In 1985, the Appellate Division sustained much of Kenford’s reliance and mitigation recovery, rejected some expenses and DSI’s lost profits, and ordered a new trial on the amount of land appreciation. Its majority allowed that category but rejected valuation assumptions involving a theme park, offices, and golf course. The retrial was to compare raw acreage value after stadium construction with purchase value. Two justices dissented on foreseeability and speculation.

In a separate earlier appeal, the Court of Appeals rejected DSI’s management profits because the parties had not contemplated liability for them and the proof was too speculative. The land retrial then yielded $6.5 million. The Appellate Division affirmed in 1988; two justices concurred only because its 1985 recoverability ruling was law of the case.

The County’s appeal from the final order brought up the necessarily affecting 1985 nonfinal order under Civil Practice Law and Rules § 5601(d). Other orders the County sought to challenge were outside that review route. The pertinent question was whether it had assumed liability for the missing appreciation.

sections.title: Shared expectations do not establish an assumed investment guarantee
sections.cue: What did the contract make the County responsible for?
paragraphs: Designated Judge Mollen explained that ordinary damages compensate natural and probable consequences, while extraordinary losses require contemplation at or before formation as a probable result of breach. Contractual nature, purpose, known circumstances, and liability consciously assumed or reasonably conveyed to the other party all inform that inquiry.

Kenford stressed that higher assessments and peripheral tax revenues were explicit contractual expectations and that everyone anticipated an economic boom. The court agreed that appreciation was foreseen, but distinguished anticipating a benefit from promising compensation if it failed to materialize. The revenue terms did not transfer Kenford’s investment risk to the County.

The earlier management-profits decision illustrated the same limit: default remedies had not contemplated such heavy responsibility, and evidence did not show the parties would have accepted it if expressly considered. Kenford, moreover, had no contractual duty to buy or retain peripheral land; its obligation concerned the 178-acre donation. County knowledge of extra purchases did not itself incorporate their special consequences into the bargain.

The court compared precedents involving sugar supply, delayed telegrams, and the broken mill shaft in Hadley, each illustrating limits on extraordinary losses absent adequate connection to the assumed obligation. Kenford voluntarily pursued surrounding-land gains. Without a transfer of risk, it could benefit from construction or lose expected appreciation if construction failed. Its theory effectively guaranteed the gain in either event, without contractual or evidentiary support. Limiting unassumed risks also reduced business uncertainty.

sections.title: The appreciation award is struck rather than recalculated
sections.cue: How far did the reversal reach?
paragraphs: The Court of Appeals held peripheral-land appreciation unrecoverable as a matter of law because the County had not reasonably contemplated liability for it. It struck the award, rather than ordering another valuation trial. This ruling rested on assumed liability, without separately deciding that the retrial appraisal failed reasonable certainty.

The five participating judges reversed the relevant portions of the 1988 final order and 1985 order, with costs. Chief Judge Wachtler and Judges Alexander, Titone, and Bellacosa joined Mollen. Judges Simons, Kaye, and Hancock did not participate, and there was no separate writing. Other damages surviving the long litigation were not all vacated.
